Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X83/X83n1578.xml). Records Pointing at the Moon: Jiufeng Daoqian bears the exact headword. Jiufeng defines inner succession as knowing how to take responsibility within.

Senses.Explanation: Inner succession is the inward side of the royal-line analogy used in Five-Ranks discourse. Jiufeng Daoqian defines it as knowing how to take responsibility within, distinguishes it from outer succession in the minister’s position, and still places the royal seed beyond both taking responsibility and carrying a burden. In Jiufeng Daoqian’s exchange, a questioner asks whether outward succession is the minister’s position and inward succession the royal seed. Jiufeng accepts the setup, then defines outer and inner succession separately before refusing to equate inner succession with the royal seed itself. The Records Pointing at the Moon and the Compendium of the Five Lamps preserve that same explicit definition, while the Complete Collection and Strict Lineage repeat the case in separate works. Hongzhi Zhengjue uses ‘inner succession arriving home’ opposite ‘branching off and borrowing the road’ in a public address. Yongjue Yuanxian distinguishes royal-prince Five Ranks as internally divided into inner and outer succession. The corpus therefore gives a technical relation, not a generic synonym for transmission.

Occurrences.Kwic: 慧是定用。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2008.xml). Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch. Speaker: Huineng. In his address on stability and insight, Huineng says that insight is stability's use, that each is present in the other, and that treating them as separate or sequential makes two where he says there is one.

Senses.Explanation: Insight is the capacity for clear seeing that the records place beside discipline and stability, then test as a question in the public interview. Huineng says that insight is stability's use and that each is present in the other; he rejects treating them as separate or sequential. This gives the pair a stated relation without collapsing their different lexical jobs. Asked directly what insight is, Tian'an Sheng answers with the four directions distinctly marked, Ruibai Mingxue with light already pervading, Shipu Chaozhi by asking whether it can be deceived, and Jiguang Huo with cold light piercing its case and all smoke and dust cut off. These replies keep clarity observable without reducing the word to an abstract formula. Other masters refuse a fixed explanatory object. Wufeng Ruxue moves the whisk, Zizhou Chuan holds up his staff, Yezhu Fuhui refuses to tell, and Shenfeng Xian calls himself muddle-headed. Shishuang Erzhan points to a large stone Buddha, while Changmu Guangdian gives peach blossoms in spring and plum blossoms in winter. The word remains one capacity; different replies test how it is shown. The related graph commonly translated as discernment overlaps in ordinary English, but its installed entry is grounded in contrast with discriminating consciousness. This graph is retained only where speakers ask for or display the clear-seeing capacity itself. The evidence does not license merging the graphs or splitting this entry merely because English can call both ‘wisdom.’

Senses.Explanation: Oxherding pictures are illustrated and versified Chan sequences that arrange the ox-and-herder image into named stages; the corpus preserves more than one ten-picture order and also warns that diagrams can become stale goods. The Puming arrangement begins with the ox unherded, moves through initial restraint and habituation, and ends with both ox and herder forgotten. A second sequence runs from searching for the ox through finding traces, seeing and gaining it, returning home, forgetting ox and person, returning to the source, and entering the marketplace. Prefaces connect the pictures with older public ox-herding exchanges and invite readers to compare their own position. Yet Zhuhong's preface explicitly says that for someone who enters directly, the picture becomes stale merchandise and the verse surplus talk. Senses.Explanation: A child who tends cattle: a herdboy, cowherd boy, or oxherd boy. The term is attested, and Chan records concentrate its distinctive use in oxherding songs, pictures, public questions, and verse. In Puming's ten oxherding verses, the boy holds the grass rope without slack and works all day; later, when there is no ox anywhere, the boy is idle, claps, sings under the moon, and still returns to “one further barrier.” Fenyang Shanzhao's Herdboy Song says that the boy does not copy texts or read a single graph, yet unfolds countless scrolls and handles question and answer. Asked “what is the herdboy's song?” Xuefeng Yicun dances and leaves the teaching hall. Jiashan Lingquan Ziying answers “who is the person within Jiashan's scene?” with “the herdboy sings in the open fields; the woodcutter laughs deep in the clouds.” Dizang Shouen, Danxia Zichun, Hongzhi Zhengjue, and Furong Daokai further place the boy in teaching-seat and portrait verse.
